model:claude|title:discovering and explo.content_excerpt: Over the past few months, we’ve used an unreleased, internal research model to find critical vulnerabilities in some of the world’s most widely used software, such as browsers and operating systems. These attack chains demonstrate the model’s ability to create sophisticated, multi-step exploits in both open-source and proprietary software. Any vulnerabilities in these products could affect billions of users. They’re also among the most security-critical software in the world, making them a bellwether for testing models’ vulnerability research and cyber capabilities. We reported each vulnerability to the affected vendor under our coordinated vulnerability disclosure , which gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before we discuss details beyond what is already included in a public advisory. After initial prompting, Claude wrote a full exploit chain enabling an attacker to execute arbitrary code as the user, outside the browser’s sandbox. Among them are 13 sandbox escapes and 21 vulnerabilities that could have been used to compromise the renderer. The chain is interesting because it is a data-only attack that never relies on arbitrary code execution. Instead, it uses full read/write access to the browser process’s memory to modify a security flag, an object size, and a URL. model:deepseek|ver:4.1|title:zero mismat.content_excerpt: Last month, we showed that rollout and training can agree exactly. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, vLLM and the trainer produced the same logprob for every sampled token, bit for bit, on the fast kernels, with an 8.7% reduction in rollout throughput. An agent skill now does the alignment for each new model. That post was about synchronous RL, which has no weight lag, so zero mismatch removes the only gap between rollout and training. This post is about asynchronous RL, which is faster but off-policy by design. Does zero mismatch still matter there? We answer with a new paper from NVIDIA Research and Inferact (Jian Hu et al.): REINFORCE Zero: Kernel Alignment Unlocks Stable Asynchronous RL with Importance Sampling . All numbers in sections 2 to 4 come from it. In synchronous RL, rollout and training take turns, and each waits for the other. Asynchronous RL runs them at the same time: rollout keeps generating while the learner updates. The price is weight lag . A sample generated with weights version v is trained at version k > v. The gap k − v is not small: REINFORCE Zero runs at lag 2 and 8 on math reasoning, and at lag 64 on agentic tool use. So the learner always trains on samples from an older policy. The standard correction is importance sampling (IS): reweight each token by π / μ, the learner's probability for it divided by the probability the rollout recorded when it sampled it. The question is whether that correction covers the whole gap. π is the learner's computation and μ is the rollout engine's. The second term compares the two at the same weights θv. Weight lag changes smoothly. It telescopes over the most recent updates, and when each update is small it follows a smoothly changing policy trajectory. This is the gap IS is meant to correct. Kernel mismatch fluctuates. It depends on batch composition and numerical execution, so it introduces fluctuations even when rollout and learner use identical weights. Figure 1: Peak-to-median ratio of the importance-weight deviation D3, log scale, for two asynchronous runs on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: REINFORCE Zero with aligned kernels and IS with standard kernels. Source: REINFORCE Zero, Table 2. The REINFORCE Zero paper measures this with D3, the per-update average of w − 1 − log w over tokens, where w is the importance weight. model:mistral|variant:large|title:day 0.content_excerpt: We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder. Supporting it took more than a model file. ML4 runs on vLLM's model runner V2 (MRV2) with breakable CUDA graphs. Its building blocks live in a new vllm/models/mistral/ package, and the work produced generic improvements to decode context parallelism (DCP), prefill context parallelism (PCP), DSpark, NIXL-based disaggregated serving and HiSparse host-memory KV offload. Mistral Large 4 support ships in the vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 Docker image, which also includes mistral-common 1.13. The commands below run vllm serve inside it: NVFP4 does not trade quality for speed. On multimodal, long-context, agentic coding, business automation and cyber evals it stays within 2.1 points of FP8 on every task, and the mean difference is −0.3 points. Token consumption is matched too: mean completion tokens stay within about 4% of FP8. It is also faster and lighter: at TP8, NVFP4 decodes 1.08–1.19x faster per token than FP8 without spec decoding (1.18–1.22x with DSpark) and holds ~1.5x the KV cache. Long context (DCP). Add --decode-context-parallel-size 8 to shard the latent KV cache across the 8 ranks. It requires the default FP8 KV cache. Multimodal. Pass --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": N}' to allow up to N images per prompt. For multi-node, disaggregated P/D and other tested configurations, see the Mistral Large 4 recipe . Sparse MLA + DSA indexer. ML4 reuses vLLM's sparse-MLA stack (FlashMLA sparse with the fp8_ds_mla latent cache, plus the sparse indexer with an FP8 indexer cache). ML4-specific differences are layered on top: shared-indexer layers that reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, an indexer with its own SSMax, and NoPE indexers on NoPE layers. Per token, the KV cache stores 47,136 bytes: 41,328 for the MLA latent and 5,808 for the indexer. Cross-layer KV sharing. Nine NoPE layers read the latent KV written by layer 35 instead of writing their own. We added kv_sharing_target_layer_name to MLAAttention and AttentionLayerBase . model:vllm|title:introducing kinference.content_excerpt: We’re excited to announce Kinference [kay-inference] , a new open source project for building scalable inference platforms with vLLM. We created Kinference at Buoyant after watching our customers struggle to run open weight models in their environments. We designed Kinference to be the control plane layer for the platform you need to build. It uses vLLM to do the underlying inference, and provides the set of features necessary for building an inference platform in practice. This includes token rate limiting, tenant usage and cost tracking, intelligent load balancing, and inference policies. Kinference can be paired with your existing stack. Using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there. Kinference serves a heterogeneous, evolving set of models running on a heterogeneous, evolving pool of GPUs, to a heterogenous, evolving set of clients.. In addition to policies and a routing layer, Kinference provides inference-specific load balancing that takes into account signals like GPU queue sizes, historical performance, and the contents of the KV cache on the GPU. This KV-cache awareness, in particular, allows Kinference to send requests to the vLLM worker that will do the least work for that specific request. Modeling the KV cache content of the GPU can produce dramatic gains in performance for distributed inference. For example, in our public Kinference benchmarks , we showed that, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing (labeled “service” below), Kinference (labeled “kinference”) was able to cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type. By incorporating cache awareness into policies, platform owners can create policies that will send simple requests to the cheaper model — but only if that’s less work than sending them to the expensive model in the first place. In our unloaded latency benchmark above, we sought to measure the effect of Kinference’s KV-cache-aware load balancing in isolation. In our capacity benchmark, below, we measured the requests per minute can each endpoint can serve within a latency SLO. In the capacity benchmark, Kinference served 7.4× the goodput on shared-prefix and about 3.5× the goodput on multiturn . model:vllm|ver:3.1|variant:pro|title:vll.content_excerpt: Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's most capable open-weight model: a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context that matches the strongest closed-source models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs. Each sparse attention layer has a small indexer next to its MLA attention. The indexer keeps one FP8 key per token (132 bytes with its scale) and scores every earlier token for each query with 32 lightweight heads. Then it keeps the top 2,048 tokens. MLA attention then runs exactly, but only over those 2,048 tokens. DSA was introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2; our DeepSeek-V3.2 post covers the indexer in more detail. The payoff is largest in long-context decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth. Dense MLA reads 576 bytes of FP8 latent per context token per layer. DSA still scans the whole context, but only the 132-byte index keys. It then reads the full latent for just 2,048 tokens. At long context, that is about 23% of the bytes dense MLA reads per layer. Figure 1: Sparse attention (DSA) in Kimi K3.1 Pro. The indexer scores every past token, keeps the top 2,048, and every query head attends exactly over only those tokens' latents. Step through it. The index keys are a second per-token cache next to the MLA latent. Under tensor parallelism (TP) both are replicated on every GPU; KDA state is per request, as in K3. The latent and the index keys can be quantized independently. An NVFP4 latent alone already brings K3.1 Pro below K3 with FP8. Opt-in MXFP4 index keys fit 11% more tokens on top and make the indexer 10–20% faster at long context. With both, eight GB300 GPUs hold 1.7× as many tokens as with FP8, and DCP8 multiplies that by seven: about 36 full 1M-token contexts at once, against 3 for TP8 with FP8. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. Arca's head of AI discusses persistent memory, the benefits of a custom harness, and agentic workflows that span days. At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh , the lead AI Engineer at Arca , an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. “So we have this persistence for every client ,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness , which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic,” he said. “And they take the decision making off the agent's hands.”

story|title:ai agent has amnesia mine ke.content_excerpt: Months of shared memory across Claude, Codex and Antigravity — versions, retractions, and why append-only notes keep failing TL;DR. Scattered Markdown notes kept sending my agents down paths we had already rejected. I built a shared Git-backed store (KYB) with versioned records and lifecycle states — active, archived, retracted. Query current state, history, or a time slice separately; replace wrong text instead of appending; separate finished work from wrong knowledge. Pinned to KYB v0.3.3, no controlled benchmarks — mechanisms and field notes below. Before KYB, my coding agents already had memory: Markdown files scattered across different places. The flaw showed up whenever another agent returned to a workspace, found an older note, and mistook it for the active plan. In my experience, an agent would sometimes spend hours pursuing an approach we had already investigated and rejected. The file still held a perfectly reasonable case for the old approach, while the decision to abandon it lived somewhere else. I am Alexander Panasenko, the author of KYB (Know Your Business), so I have a stake in this story: it is my open-source project. This is an account of my engineering experience with Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Google Antigravity from summer through October 2026. The text, its translation, and the diagrams were prepared with AI assistance, based on my own experience, the public source code, and saved development records. A fresh session does not automatically inherit the conversation that just ended. A human had to step in and explain which file still mattered, why we changed course, and where the outcome was recorded. An obvious temptation is to write one more summary note, but that note needs remembering too: without updates, it goes stale like the rest. So here is the question this piece addresses: how do you preserve operational knowledge across sessions without letting an outdated note send the next agent down a path you already abandoned? My short answer is to save a little, with versions and lifecycle state, and keep three things apart: what is true now, what was recorded then, and how an attempt ended. Weight-Space Programming: Frontier Models Reading and Writing Neural Network Weights Core claim and replications : Several groups report that frontier LLMs can generate or edit small networks' weights directly, without gradient training or tools. Cross-generation replication : Alex Krentsel's replication of MIT's experiment found a sharp capability jump across model generations; the latest models generated Breakout networks scoring up to 22× an RL-trained baseline ( summary ). story|title:artificial analysis v5 and t.content_excerpt: Hill-climbing is easy, knowing what to hill-climb is hard. Making scores go up is expensive , but we have a much clearer playbook for it than we do for creating meaningful benchmarks at the true frontier of AI today. Independent evaluation of language models is under-appreciated in how hard of a task it is. These groups are not just taking current models and certifying their scores, which is a technically involved task. This is their job if AI progress is slow. When AI progress is as fast as it is, the technical details of the job are the routine work part of trying to put a single number on what makes for a good AI model today. The goal is to have a single number that is representative of current models, matching vibe checks, community sentiment, and scientific analysis, while being forward looking enough so that it’s not outdated in 3 months. Everyone building a benchmark faces a sort of paradox. You need your benchmark to reduce to one single number, so that it is easy to discuss, use in reports, and compare models, but every method of aggregating scores comes with meaningful trade-offs. The best scientists need to do this, everyone does. It’s a matter of creating aggregation metrics that you think are most fair, knowing there will always be imperfections. With the amount of money in the AI ecosystem today, the weight of independent evaluation is even higher – you dictate the winners and losers of a trillion dollar market. You also influence some of the models themselves, steering the shape of progress. This is a lot of pressure! My prompt for this article is Artificial Analysis’s recent update to their Intelligence Index, v5 . In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE , a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task. OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing. However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record. Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database. A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem. So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. story|title:gdpx measuring frontier mode.content_excerpt: GDPx is a benchmark that covers the most valuable domains for frontier intelligence. It aims to be the world’s best benchmark for measuring general agentic capabilities. We believe the first trillion dollars of AI revenue will be concentrated in sectors that can deploy frontier intelligence at high ROI , not broadly diffused throughout the whole economy. Building a general-purpose benchmark based on share of GDP or the SOC/O*NET occupational taxonomy is therefore a mistake. If your goal is to track the progress of frontier models, you should focus on the domains where they will be most impactful. It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. If we exclude cyber, biology, and alignment—the three domains where safety classifiers sometimes kick in—you get the following results instead. We were pleasantly surprised by how well this ranking lines up with our subjective impression of the models. OpenAI and Anthropic generally dominate the top of the ranking while SpaceXAI, Meta, and open-weight models are all meaningfully behind. Gemini 4 Carbon is a real improvement from Google and the only model in the same ballpark as Opus and Astra. It will be interesting to see people’s impressions once Carbon becomes generally available. We believe it’s underrated how relevant safety classifiers are when picking the best model for certain use cases. For example, Muse Wonder Full is actually the best available cyber model today by a meaningful margin . Opus 5.5 is the best all-around model and wins in quant trading, hardware design, and chip design. Gemini 4 Carbon is the best bio model (likely due to weaker safety classifiers) and edges out the win in software engineering. GPT-6 Astra wins convincingly for RSI and is also the best model for materials science. Our finance and legal tasks are so challenging that basically every model scores exactly 0. Interestingly, if you subset to a single model family, you will sometimes see very similar spikes. The cost vs performance Pareto frontier also matches our general experience using the models: Luna and DeepSeek fight for the low end, Opus wins the high end, and OpenAI claims the middle. Again, however, the appearance of Gemini 4 Carbon is worth watching closely. It’s impossible to make all the nuanced comparisons enabled by GDPx in a single newsletter. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. story|title:how to build evidence ground.content_excerpt: Agents working across an organization’s policies, manuals, wikis, tickets, and code must navigate knowledge scattered across systems and teams. Finding a relevant passage is only the start. They also need to determine which rules apply, what has changed, and how one source affects another. A persistent memory layer preserves knowledge and relationships for agents to reuse across tasks. Without it, agents often have to reconstruct that understanding on every question, making their work expensive and error-prone. This is especially challenging in banking and insurance, where policies and guidelines frequently amend or supersede one another. We tested OpenWiki , our open-source wiki compiler, as this memory layer. On questions requiring connections across sources, the wiki made the agent roughly 5x more accurate than search alone. Adding an evidence graph that connects wiki statements to supporting passages and links related sources improved accuracy a further 27% and doubled citation consistency. RAG pipelines often use semantic or hybrid search to retrieve isolated chunks, leaving agents to piece together how those chunks relate. We’ve explored improving retrieval with agentic RAG and graph-based metadata filtering , but finding relevant passages is only part of the work. Cross-source questions require tracing references, resolving conflicting rules, and understanding dependencies. Memory preserves that understanding so agents don’t have to rebuild it on every question. A compiled wiki provides that memory layer by synthesizing source material into linked pages that explain key concepts and their relationships. The wiki is updated as sources change, giving agents context they can reuse. OpenWiki , our open-source CLI built on Deep Agents , creates these wikis with citations back to the sources. We originally built it so coding agents wouldn’t have to rediscover architecture and code behavior on every task. Every OpenWiki statement rests on a claim , an assertion linked to supporting source lines and their hash. When those lines change, the hash changes, allowing OpenWiki to flag affected claims without a model call, saving on token costs and making staleness detection more deterministic. Only those claims go to a model for confirmation, revision, or retraction, allowing the memory layer to self-correct as its sources change. story|title:how we optimized browser use.content_excerpt: Browser agents can now take on multi-step work that's painful and time-consuming for people. Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse plan cross-country road trips, cancel unused subscriptions, and list cars for sale, all on sites with no public APIs. DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Browser use helps in two places: actions an API can't cover, like using a website the agent wasn't set up for, and end-to-end testing of the web apps coding agents build. Either way, the agent needs two things: This post focuses on the tools, and on making them good enough that the agent uses the browser well. We set out to give agents in Managed Deep Agents a browser. We compared seven toolsets and picked the best one, Stagehand ( GitHub ) from Browserbase . Then we improved it based on what agents did in LangSmith traces, and validated every change with evals. The biggest lesson was how much room there is to improve an agent through tool design. Browser use toolsets come in a few forms: native tools, an MCP server , or a CLI the agent runs in a shell. Browser use poses two unique challenges for those tools: We iterated with the agent development lifecycle : run the agent on a benchmark, read its traces in LangSmith to see where it wasted steps or tokens, change the tool, and run evals to check that the change helped. Every run was a LangSmith experiment , so we could compare setups side by side and click from any number into the trace behind it. We had every harness return structured output (a JSON answer). That way a formatting slip, like a one-line reply to a task that asks for a table, didn't count against its browsing. We upstreamed that option to Browserbase's evals. We first held the model and tasks fixed and changed only the toolset. The seven toolsets differ in how the agent calls them: Every toolset passed between 78% and 90% of tasks, but cost and speed varied widely. The Stagehand tools passed the most (90%) for $1.98 in total, at a median 17.4 s per task. Playwright MCP passed 78% for $26.71, about 13x the cost, and took three times as long per task ( full results ). The gap held on harder tasks. On HardBench's 38 core tasks, Deep Agents passed 30 with Stagehand's code-writing run tool and 21 with Browserbase's command-style browse CLI, at three times the cost per task. Your traces, evals, datasets, prompts, and agent deployments stay in your own cloud account, on the cloud you choose, and LangChain manages the data plane for you, from orchestration and scaling to platform updates. By splitting the control plane and data plane in two, BYOC provides greater flexibily to decide where agents run and where telemetry lives, without taking on the work of running LangSmith. LangChain runs the control plane , which holds auth, org and workspace config, billing metadata, hashed API keys, and static UI assets. You own the data plane , which holds everything sensitive, from traces, prompts, and datasets to experiments, agent deployments, and workspace secrets. An organization can hold several data planes, each in its specific account and region, and each data plane holds its workspaces. This lets you split data planes by region, environment, or business unit. For example, a platform team might run production and staging data planes in separate AWS accounts, while a business unit that standardized on Azure runs its own, separate BYOC deployment on Azure. Each team's traces land in the account that team owns. Until now, teams with strict compliance boundaries deployed and maintained self-hosted LangSmith. This kept their data inside their own boundary, but it took dedicated platform engineers to patch stateful services, configure databases, and run schema migrations. story|title:new context engineering chal.content_excerpt: It feels like everyone is converging on the same agent architecture: an LLM, running in a loop, calling tools, running in a sandbox. Claude Code - perhaps the first high profile manifestation of this - came out over a year and a half ago. Deep Agents , our agent harness, launched over a year ago. This pattern has been building for a while. There’s nothing bad with that convergence per se, but it has led to a sentiment among some AI engineers that I’ve talked to recently that “all the hard problems are solved” or “there’s no new AI engineering problems to solve”. When people express this sentiment, I think they are largely talking about the context engineering practices we do to make agents work. And to some extent they are right - there are a lot of standard-ish context engineering solutions we’ve all arrived at: The good news (for context engineering aficionados like myself) is that I think we’re seeing a step function change in agent capabilities, or at least how they are being used. Specifically, over the past few months every agent builder I’ve chatted with has been thinking about proactive, always on, goal-oriented agents . The core of this agent shares a lot of similarities with coding agents, but there are a set of new challenges as well. I highlight a few below. We (at LangChain, and in the industry) don’t necessarily have solutions (or at least, general solutions) for these, so thinking about these has been the most fun I’ve had in a while! How to be proactive without being annoying : These proactive agents run in the background and either listen to event feeds or are woken up with heartbeats. On one hand, they need to be able to push things to the user - that creates a sense of helping. On the other hand, if you push too many notifications to the user, you risk overwhelming them. Calibrating this to be a delightful experience (not too much, not too little) is still a hard context engineering challenge! Memory : Memory for agents has been something we’ve talked with builders about for a while. Memory systems end up having two parts: the underlying data structure and an intelligence layer (agent) around the data. The data structures are often pretty simple ( files , a single string). The hardest part of the intelligence layer is figuring out what to remember. story|title:statebench testing how langu.content_excerpt: We’re introducing StateBench , a benchmark for long-context state tracking —how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve. State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack. Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds. To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer. StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. Today we are excited to announce the launch of XLA Serving Engine (XSE) , a general-purpose model export and inference runtime for the OpenXLA ecosystem , open-sourced under the Apache 2.0 license. We created XLA Serving Engine to enable a “Train in Python, Serve in C++” workflow. Most ML engineers develop models using Python (with frameworks like JAX and PyTorch); however, some production serving environments do not allow Python due to operational and deployment complexity. XLA Serving Engine offers a solution by providing an API for engineers to export their ML models to an “XLA SavedModel” containing the StableHLO representation of their model’s function, which can then be loaded and executed by the XLA Serving Runtime. This approach allows users to serve models (typically non-LLMs) directly in a C++ runtime, which enables high throughput at any scale and optimizes for low latency by removing the overhead of the Python interpreter. In our studies , we found that for short requests, XSE delivers 2–5x the throughput of the best Python server we could build, and 8–36x that of a straightforward one, while using 30–70% less CPU time per prediction and a quarter of the memory. Last year, we began deploying core components of XLA Serving Engine as part of Google’s internal load-bearing, production serving infrastructure. Today, XSE serves over 6 million queries per second and powers some of Google's highest-volume online inference pipelines, including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, Search, and parts of Gemini Omni, with plans to onboard more customers internally. Having successfully scaled XSE to support the high-throughput workloads of our internal teams, we are now ready to bring this core piece of infrastructure to the wider ecosystem of hardware partners and Cloud TPU users. We designed XLA Serving Engine to be self-contained and modular, so users can deploy it as a standalone inference engine or plug it into their more complex serving solutions. Our Private Preview partners have been actively leveraging XLA Serving Engine to bring their deep learning stacks to production. story|title:the elephant goldfish model.content_excerpt: The latest news from Google on open source releases, major projects, events, and outreach programs for early career developers. by Brian Suchy , Jim Quinn , Elise Ewing , Oliver Newth and Dave Rensin on behalf of the Elephant-Goldfish Model team AI-powered velocity is transformative; however, it has silently introduced a potential reliability crisis by also increasing the velocity of “slop,” bugs, and session context collapse. Generative AI tools excel at increasing coding speed, but pure speed without structured guardrails means we are often auto-scaling our mistakes rather than simply writing code faster. We need a paradigm shift, aligning the human need for system comprehension with AI’s capacity for execution. As co-author Dave Rensin outlines in the article Elephants, Goldfish, and the New Golden Age of Software Engineering , “Design is the new code.” The EGM framework is a metaphor for a powerful way to develop AI-assisted software quickly and safely with humans intentionally in the loop. The “Elephant” is a context-rich, long-horizon AI session that holds the end-to-end architectural vision and project memory. No code is written here; it is purely dedicated to design, intent, and capturing micro-decisions. The Elephant session is where the AI interviews you and you debate the merits of your choices. Conversely, “Goldfish” are stateless, zero-context sessions used strictly to validate specifications. Because they share no “blind spots” with the designer, they act as objective critics, probing for gaps and edge cases. The goal of this method is for the AI to correctly produce the code you wanted the first time after you press Enter. To put this methodology into practice at scale, we are thrilled to announce the Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin . Originally, this plugin was developed internally for Google software engineers, and is now open source. Thousands of Googlers use this plugin every day to ship production Google code. Released under the Apache 2.0 license, the repository provides everything you need to implement this framework. Developers will find customizable Markdown rules, defined subagent personas, and structured review workflows ready to integrate into your own environments. The plugin’s core goal is to bring the EGM framework directly into Antigravity, with other development environments upcoming. story|title:the iron wood throne google.content_excerpt: In November 2025, we published a newsletter saying that Google is selling TPUs to external customers. Since then, we have been proven right over and over again with Oracle, OpenAI , Anthropic, and Meta all becoming customers of TPUs just as our Accelerator Model reported. Hardware demand is only half the story, as NVIDIA’s moat has historically been its software and large developer ecosystem. This is where TPU is also making headway, partnering with upstream maintainers across the entire ecosystem, including the Meta PyTorch team, vLLM (Inferact, RedHat), SGLang (RadixArk), llm-d, Ray, etc. This is not a surprise to folks that have read our September 2026 article laying out Google TPU’s externalization strategy . Back in our September article, we published the first third-party TPUv7 results on InferenceX on single-turn workloads, showing that in an apples-to-apples FP8 comparison on Qwen 3.5 397B, TPUv7 Ironwood) delivered up to 50% better performance per dollar than B200 and B300. We also reported that many Google TPU customers were asking for AgentX results, since long-context, multi-turn agentic serving is where inference spend is heading. story|title:toyblocks a controlled world.content_excerpt: Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails. To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure. Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control. Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks : an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking. ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training. Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments. Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2 , MolmoBot , and MolmoSpaces , ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain. As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain. story|title:why agents are soon only goi.content_excerpt: For the past two years, building capable Agents meant designing tools, figuring out which actions help the model complete a task, deciding how granular each tool schema needs to be, or iterating on system instruction templates. This is changing. Agents are moving in the opposite direction by collapsing their entire tool catalog into one tool : exec . This is called Code Mode (or Programmatic Tool Calling). Instead of forcing the model to trigger tools one at a time across turns, the harness gives the model a single exec(code) tool. The model writes a short TypeScript or Python script that chains, combines, and awaits actions inside an isolated sandbox. To understand why agents are converging on a single exec tool, we should look at how tool calling evolved. Initially, we only gave agents a handful of tools because they couldn't reliably choose or filter across a large catalog. As models improved, we connected dozens of tools or MCP servers, but ran into context window limits. We solved that with tool search and progressive disclosure , letting agents look up tools on demand. Even with dynamic tool loading, we still had dozens of individual tools, and were still stuck with the limitation of standard tool calling: one action per turn. In standard tool calling, the model generates a structured object (typically JSON) that defines a single action (or at best a flat batch of independent calls, like reading three files), waits for the raw output to come back, adds it into the prompt history, reasons again, and decides what to do next. From my own experience, we made a big jump recently in how reliably models can combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass: Several shifts came together to enable this. Frontier models are trained heavily on code, and providers have started post-training models for Code Mode. At the same time, MCP servers now increasingly ship outputSchema alongside inputSchema , giving the model upfront knowledge of return types so it can chain Tool A into Tool B inside the same script before seeing runtime output. Code Mode collapses the tool catalog into a single tool on the model surface: exec(code) . Instead of passing 80 separate JSON Schema tool objects to the model API, the agent compiles those schemas into compact type declarations ( declare namespace tools { ... } ). story|title:why human insight is a strat.content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put in his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. Every stored user message (4,972 in total) said the same thing: "hello" . The responses, however, told a very different story. They contained user identities, AWS credentials, cloud metadata probe results, process listings, network information, and credential-file paths. A closer investigation by our research team at Era, revealed a Chinese-language exploitation framework that sent a series of rapid messages, 3.5 seconds apart, each delivering malicious commands. We named the framework Greeter after its seemingly benign “hello” greetings. It exploited an old vulnerability ( CVE-2024-58351 ) in Flowise’s runtime configuration mechanism. The vulnerability allows attackers to override JavaScript instructions for some of Flowise’s API endpoints, allowing the framework to execute malicious instructions without modifying the saved chatflow. As a result, the chatflow appeared harmless, while the API was in fact used to deliver malicious instructions and return the results of their execution. The structuring of the attack, with ephemeral hello messages, is what makes it so elegant, and difficult to detect unless you’re looking for specific IoC’s in logs. The attack demonstrates how a vulnerability in an AI application can expose the underlying infrastructure, sensitive information, and cloud identities accessible to its workload. For context, Flowise is a widely-adopted open-source agentic development platform that organizations can deploy in their own cloud environments. Flowise is popular,with more than 55,000 GitHub stars and over five million Docker image pulls. Our research team recorded the attacks over two and a half months, from July to October 2026, on a network of seven Flowise honeypots across four regions. To better evaluate the real-world attack surface of Flowise deployments, we queried Shodan, a search engine that discovers internet-connected devices and services. Combining results from title:"Flowise" and product:"Flowise" , we identified 4,372 unique Flowise instances exposed to the internet. Of those, 3,277 reported a recognizable Flowise version. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements. Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). story|variant:small|title:palette teachi.content_excerpt: Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Nobody makes a deck in one pass.
